title: Norway’s household debt burden has eased, but property borrowers face different refinancing risks
summary: Norwegian households and banks enter a more uncertain global environment with stronger immediate defences than a few years ago. The Financial Stability Committee nevertheless identifies a route by which an external shock could become a domestic credit problem. A reassessment of returns on debt-financed AI investment or of heavily indebted governments could hurt securities prices. Leveraged investors facing margin or redemption pressure might then sell into less liquid markets, raising financing costs elsewhere. Norwegian banks can encounter that pressure while their borrowers are still current on loans. The report’s assessment concerns the capacity to absorb such a sequence, rather than a forecast that it will occur.

Household debt remains high internationally, but the aggregate ratio in Chart 2.1 fell from about 220% of disposable income in 2022 Q4 to 209% in 2026 Q2. The chart defines disposable income after tax and interest expenses and uses a separate scale for servicing costs. Its values from 2026 Q3 onward are projections. A decline in the ratio need not mean individual families paid down principal. Income grew faster than debt, with the decline extending across groups and especially to those that had carried the heaviest burdens. Higher rates still take cash out of monthly budgets. The Bank highlights the risk that households cut consumption sharply even when they continue servicing loans.

The distribution of accessible savings matters more for that response than aggregate wealth. Chart 2.8 estimates a negative margin for 1.91% of the homeowners in its 2025 sample, representing 2.23% of the group’s debt. The calculation lets a household draw on bank deposits to meet necessary expenses. It excludes renters and certain extreme income and debt observations, and 2025 uses preliminary tax-settlement data. The estimate is about capacity to absorb expenditure at a specified standard, not actual arrears. Increases in listed shares and fund holdings also include valuation gains, which can disappear during the market shock in which cash is needed.

Property developers and owners of occupied buildings face different cash flows. Developers must fund construction until buyers commit, and high building and financing costs have made potential projects harder to justify. An owner with tenants can earn rent and cover interest while the property’s valuation falls. Competition among lenders and some equity-financed purchases have helped support commercial property prices, but limited rental growth and higher longer-term rates weigh on valuations. Chart 3.14 shows relatively flat projected selling prices, revised down from the preceding assessment. The special feature on Oslo finds that an increasing share of the value of new homes is attributable to land-related values. Those are estimates, and a lower residual land value changes the economics of future development even if construction costs stay high.

Chart 3.16 shows why the distinction between borrowers matters to a bank. Domestic non-performing loans in 2026 Q2 accounted for 4.59% of lending to real estate developers, 1.25% of lending to commercial property owners and 1.83% across firms. Chart 3.15 reports recognised losses on a different basis, annualising the 2026 quarterly flows. A non-performing loan is not a realised loss of its full principal. Banks still met capital and liquidity requirements by ample margins. The countercyclical buffer remained at 2.5%. Capital headroom helps maintain lending if losses emerge, while borrowers’ contractual maturities, liquid assets and access to replacement funding determine how rapidly stress reaches their balance sheets.

questions.question: Which households would cut spending first if rates rose and market-valued savings fell together?
questions.detail: Use the household tax and deposit data behind Chapter 2, retaining the sample exclusions and separating cash from equity and fund holdings. Compare after-tax income, contractual debt service and necessary expenses by income, age and leverage. A bank equity or consumer-credit investor needs to know whether spending falls primarily among its own customers or among households that carry little debt.

questions.question: How much property debt will need refinancing before rents or presales can adjust?
questions.detail: Compare borrower filings, bond maturity schedules and banks’ commercial property disclosures. Separate owners of occupied offices from developers financing projects before sale. Estimate coverage at the reset interest rate and collateral value at the refinancing date, allowing for existing hedges and vacant space. The same fall in an appraisal can leave a funded landlord liquid while preventing a developer from completing a project.

questions.question: Could a rise in foreign funding costs curtail domestic credit before loan losses increase?
questions.detail: Read bank funding plans alongside liquidity disclosures and the official capital-buffer decision. Examine maturity concentrations, currency hedges, collateral calls and available unencumbered assets under a common shock. Compare short-term capacity to roll funding against capital available to absorb eventual credit impairment. These channels imply different risks for covered bonds, senior bank debt and equity.
